name: Salicylic acid + sulfur

lead:
Salicylic acid and sulfur are two over-the-counter skincare ingredients often combined in spot treatments and masks for blemish-prone skin. Salicylic acid is a beta-hydroxy acid that exfoliates inside pores; sulfur has a long history as a skin remedy.
The appearance goal is clearer skin with fewer pimples and less congestion. The 2024 American Academy of Dermatology acne guideline gives salicylic acid a conditional recommendation, while benzoyl peroxide and retinoids get strong ones.

paras: Users dab the product on individual blemishes or leave it on as a mask for a limited time, then rinse. It is commonly used in an evening routine and often alongside moisturiser. Forum users also use salicylic acid cleansers.

Dryness, peeling, stinging and irritation are the usual effects, and one looksmax.org poster reported that a salicylic acid cleanser coincided with a flare of irritated, pimply skin. Sulfur has a characteristic smell. People who are pregnant or on prescription acne treatments typically ask a clinician about acids.

chain: Acid exfoliates inside pores; sulfur dries and calms spots
angle.text: It is applied to pimples and blemish-prone areas to help clear them. Users reach for it as a quick spot treatment.

lead: Salicylic acid plus sulfur refers to over-the-counter acne spot treatments, masks and washes that pair two long-used skin ingredients. Salicylic acid is a beta-hydroxy acid with a keratolytic action: it loosens the outer layer of skin so pores are less likely to clog.[1] Sulfur is an old remedy with medicinal uses recorded in antiquity, including an ancient Egyptian sulfur ointment for granular eyelids mentioned in the Ebers Papyrus.[2]

People use the pairing to clear blemishes and reduce congestion, aiming for smoother, clearer-looking skin. A 2024 evidence-based acne guideline from the American Academy of Dermatology makes a conditional recommendation for topical salicylic acid and strong recommendations for benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids and some antibiotics.[3]

Published trials test salicylic acid in various forms, such as a 21-day gel study on acne and skin barrier function, rather than the sulfur combination as a product class.[4] Community discussion on looksmax.org and T Nation centres mostly on salicylic acid cleansers and washes for pimples, ingrown hairs and body acne.

paras: Salicylic acid is applied to pimples and clogged pores, and in washes, astringent pads and sprays. Wikipedia lists acne, seborrhoeic dermatitis, calluses, keratosis pilaris and dandruff among its skincare and dermatological uses.[1] It is also used as a superficial chemical peel; a 2024 review describes peels with salicylic acid, glycolic acid and others as additional or maintenance therapy in melasma.[5]
Sulfur is traditionally used in masks and spot treatments aimed at oily, blemish-prone skin, and people who combine it with salicylic acid typically do so in a single leave-on or rinse-off product.

For acne vulgaris, the AAD guideline lists salicylic acid among the conditionally recommended topicals, alongside clascoterone and azelaic acid.[3] Dermatologists also use it for warts, psoriasis and ichthyosis.[1]

Salicylic acid is lipophilic and penetrates the oil-rich lining of pores. It acts by loosening epidermal cells so that dead skin sheds and pores are less likely to plug.[1] Its parent compounds come from willow bark and similar plants; in plants the acid works as a defence hormone.[6]
Sulfur's traditional dermatological role is as a drying, peeling agent.

Willow-derived remedies were known to Hippocrates, Galen and Pliny the Elder. Edward Stone reported in 1763 that willow bark reduced fever; Johann Buchner isolated salicin in 1828; and Raffaele Piria showed in 1838 that salicin yields salicylic acid.[1] Hermann Kolbe developed an industrial synthesis in 1860, which made wide use possible.[7]

Sulfur has been used since antiquity, including as a fumigant to purify homes and as a pest-control agent described by Cato the Elder; Pliny the Elder listed a type used medicinally.[2] Traditional Chinese medicine was among its earliest practical uses.[2]

Dryness, peeling, stinging and irritation are the usual effects of topical acids and sulfur products, and sulfur has a characteristic odour. Toxicity from salicylic acid is chiefly associated with oral overdose or heavy application of strong ointments over large skin areas; Wikipedia describes a case in which a 40% ointment over about 41% of the body surface led to hemodialysis.[1]

Wikipedia reports that a 2018 kinetic assessment found aggregate cosmetic exposure well below aspirin limits, and that cosmetic use in pregnancy is not considered a significant risk.[1] In the EU, salicylic acid is classed as toxic to reproduction (category 2), is restricted in products for children under three except shampoos, and is capped at 2.0% in most non-preservative products.[1]

On looksmax.org, one poster called a salicylic acid cleanser very effective at clearing pimples, while another reported irritation and a broader breakout after three weeks of using an acne-safe salicylic cleanser; replies to that thread argued about whether it was purging or diet.[8][9] On T Nation, posters mention salicylic acid astringents for ingrown hairs, sprays and washes for body acne, and products for acne during testosterone therapy.[10][11]

The AAD guideline (18 recommendations) is a systematic review of acne treatments.[3] A 21-day prospective trial studied a salicylic acid-containing gel on acne and barrier function.[4] A randomised split-face trial combined CO2 laser with supramolecular salicylic acid for dense comedones,[12] and a randomised trial combined supramolecular salicylic acid with niacinamide in chloasma.[13] No trials of a salicylic acid and sulfur combination were found.
